title: Morfudd and the Stage Mess
markdown:
The Lyceum Community Theatre was a dusty storybook that had learned to stand up. Plaster cherubs winked from the ceiling. The air kept a faint census of old velvet and forgotten popcorn. Behind peeling curtains, in a corner that believed in right angles, sat Morfudd Buttercup’s bookshop.

Morfudd was a weasel with big ideas and a bigger need for things to be just so. He did not merely sell books. He arranged them the way a jeweller arranges stones. He ruled a neat kingdom of spines. Each morning he polished his spectacles until they had nothing left to confess, lined every volume at attention, and greeted the rare customer with a phrase that had been rehearsed in the quiet.

“A most excellent morning to you. May I recommend a tale of particular merit?”

He believed that in a messy world, good manners were a kind of art, and also a shield.

Every day his routine was a quiet song. Otis the giraffe, who was gentleness stretched to an unreasonable height, often peered through the theatre’s tall windows. His neck made a question mark against the faded posters. He could see the bigger picture: the plasterwork, the cobwebs spun into forgotten lace, the way a whole building breathed before a show. He offered Morfudd a nod, which from that altitude counted as a review.

One afternoon the air smelled of hairspray, cheap perfume, and the particular nerves of a final rehearsal. The Lyceum Talent Show filled the wings with sparkle and last-minute fixes. A magician polished a wand. A dancer lengthened already long legs. Three singers hummed as if pitch were a shy animal.

Then the theatre sneezed.

A gust found a forgotten stage door and rushed backstage with a whoosh that had not asked permission. A cardboard castle that had seen better sieges tumbled from the flies. Fake doves, convincingly feathery, burst into a panic of papier-mâché. A rubber chicken arrived like an unfunny punchline. Streamers unfurled as startled snakes. Hats made a colourful mountain on the boards. It was an avalanche of theatrical junk.

Morfudd stepped from his shop with gleaming spectacles and the calm of a man who had alphabetised worse crises. “My dear performers, a minor rearrangement of theatrical accoutrements is underway. Please proceed with your routines, and your poise, if you would be so kind.”

He sounded like a captain announcing that the ship was only practising sinking. Otis sighed from the window, counting falling feathers with worried eyes.

Mrs. Higgins, whose voice usually boomed like a kindly foghorn, began to squeak. “The lights! The main stage lights are wobbling. They’ll fall. The show is ruined. Opening night is tomorrow.”

Morfudd adjusted his spectacles as if a better prescription might steady the rigging. “A moment of dramatic tension. Let us embrace it. I shall prepare a brief statement on the resilience of the artistic spirit, should the worst occur.” He straightened a fallen bouquet of plastic flowers and tried to make the mess look intended.

The stage became an obstacle course of near-misses. A juggler clipped the rubber chicken and sent his balls into a frantic unplanned orbit. A ballerina mid-twirl found herself married to a net of sequins. Morfudd, in the middle of it, instructed a hurried stagehand on the proper way to retrieve a runaway banjo. His voice was a low murmur of polite disapproval, a teaspoon of order in a pot of noise.

Things went on falling. Fabric rustled in a panic. The fake doves chirped their one available emotion. The rubber chicken, by a talent all its own, landed on Morfudd’s perfectly neat fur and stayed there.

“Rather an unexpected hat,” Morfudd observed. “A touch too modern for this production.”

Otis watched from his high quiet and did not laugh, though the chicken deserved it. From up there the wobbling lights were not a metaphor. They were lamps on a tired bar, shivering.

In the shouting, a small figure stepped from the shadows near the wings. Lily had been given the unglamorous job of sorting old costume ribbons. While everyone else flailed, she had been watching the lights. She held a coiled length of strong twine, found in a dusty prop box that nobody else had had time to notice.

“Excuse me,” she said, soft and clear. “These lights just need this tied here. It will hold them.”

She did not wait for a speech about artistic spirit. She crossed the scattered props with small sure feet. Her knots were neat, the sort of knots that do not need an audience. The bar settled. The stage remembered it was a floor.

Morfudd still believed in manners. Some habits sit on a shelf like favourite books and refuse to be remaindered. But he looked at Lily’s twine, then at the chicken, then at the plastic flowers he had wasted time arranging, and something in his neat kingdom loosened.

He began to notice quieter things: the rustle of a forgotten script, the sigh of the old curtains, the way Otis’s shadow made a long, kind comma across the stalls.

Otis smiled. From his height he could see the change arriving in his friend the way late sun arrives on plaster cherubs — not a proclamation, just warmth, finding the dust and making it briefly golden.

Ever since then, Morfudd still lined up his spines each morning. He also left a length of spare twine under the counter, in case the theatre sneezed again, and greeted Lily, when she came for ribbons, as if she were the most particular merit in the building.
characters: Morfudd Buttercup (an ambitious weasel bookseller), Otis (a giraffe friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
